papers.title: From Biological Curves to Soft Modular Robots: Learning-Based Inverse Design with Uncertainty-Guided Refinement
papers.abstract: Animals exhibit diverse shape-changing behaviors, from the undulatory swimming of eels to the arching movements of inchworms. Reproducing these biological shapes with modular soft robots offers a promising approach to developing versatile bioinspired robotic systems. However, translating a desired shape into a feasible robotic configuration remains challenging. Existing cable-driven modular soft robots rely on computationally expensive physics-based modeling and combinatorial search for inverse design, making it difficult to efficiently reproduce diverse target shapes. To address this challenge, we present a learning-based real-to-sim-to-real framework that translates biological curves into robotic configurations through surrogate-assisted inverse design and uncertainty-guided refinement. The proposed method combines learned inverse prediction with targeted candidate exploration, using a fast forward surrogate to evaluate and select suitable designs. The learned forward surrogate reduces deformation prediction time from $1.53 \times 10^5$ ms to 0.0008 ms, achieving approximately a $1.9 \times 10^8$-fold speedup. At the same time, the proposed inverse design method reduces design time from $1.99 \times 10^6$ ms to 4.18 ms. On 5,000 test samples generated from previously unseen threading patterns, the method achieves a 93% shape reconstruction success rate under surrogate-based evaluation. Physical demonstrations with four bioinspired robots further illustrate the translation of biological curves into realizable robotic shapes.

papers.title: SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models
papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) enable world models to plan from images by predicting future embeddings. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly incorporate task-relevant state information, so the physical state that determines task progress may not be reliably captured in the latent space. Supervising world models with simulator state can make planning more informative, but it requires deciding which state features matter. Features are typically selected by hand or weighted uniformly, and a uniform weighting gives every standardized state feature equal influence, so redundant coordinates can overcount the same variation, while irrelevant ones can obscure task-relevant differences. To address this limitation, we propose SWIM (State Weighting with Inverse-Dynamics Model), which learns state weights from offline trajectories by predicting recorded actions from current states and observed future displacements. The learned weights quantify each feature's contribution to action prediction and define a weighted state metric for state-supervised training, which we demonstrate by aligning latent and state distances. The inverse-dynamics model is used only during training, so the resulting world model plans from images with no additional planning-time computation. Across five simulated robotic manipulation tasks, SWIM consistently improves planning success over uniform state weighting.

papers.title: Mimetic Embodiment Transfer of Human-Humanoid Interaction from In-the-Wild Videos
papers.abstract: Enabling a humanoid to interact naturally with human partners requires preserving not only individual motions but also the spatial, semantic, and contact relationships underlying the interaction (i.e., hugging, dancing, hand-shaking, etc.). Furthermore, a practical solution should generalize across various humanoid embodiments with distinct morphologies and kinematic constraints. To tackle this challenge, we propose HumiTransfer, a mimetic embodiment transfer framework that converts in-the-wild human-human interaction videos into physically plausible human-humanoid interactions. HumiTransfer first reconstructs 3D human motion with consistent foot-ground contact, then transfers one participant to a target humanoid embodiment via interaction modeling, using weighted joint-relative directions and anatomical offsets to prioritize interaction-critical inter-body relationships, while post-retargeting optimization enforces balance, contact, and collision avoidance. Subsequently, we apply HumiTransfer to 1,200 in-the-wild videos, producing approximately 500,000 frames of diverse interactions for the 26-DoF Unitree R1 Edu and the 23-DoF HighTorque Mini-hi humanoid robot, resulting in our HumiMimic dataset. Across both robots, HumiTransfer achieves superior motion fidelity, preserves inter-body relationships, and maintains contact accuracy compared with existing baselines. Moreover, we demonstrate that HumiMimic supports motion generation methods for synthesizing interactive humanoid motions following a human partner. Finally, our real robot deployments confirm the physical executability of the transferred motions in real-world settings.

papers.title: Camera-to-Quadruped Robot Pose Estimation from Sequential Images
papers.abstract: Quadruped robots are increasingly deployed in hazardous environments such as disaster response and facility inspection, where external-camera monitoring is essential for safe operation. This setting is challenging because quadrupeds are articulated systems with time-varying leg joints, leg symmetry, and frequent self-occlusions, which make keypoint correspondence ambiguous. Moreover, no public benchmark exists, making quantitative comparison difficult. To address these challenges, we propose QuadPose, which estimates the full-body 18-DoF pose (6-DoF base pose + 12-DoF joint angles) from monocular video sequences, and introduce QuadSyn, the first camera-to-quadruped robot pose benchmark. On QuadSyn, QuadPose achieves 92.18% PCK@2.5px, 95.54% PCK-AUC, 85.94% ADD@20cm, 66.98% ADD-AUC, and 3.65 degree mean joint-angle error at approximately 33 FPS.

papers.title: OpenJaws: An Open Hardware UMI Framework with Stereo Localization for Generalist Manipulation
papers.abstract: Handheld data-collection interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) allow manipulation demonstrations to be gathered in the wild without a robot in the loop, but the quality of the resulting action labels is bounded by the accuracy of vision-based localization. Existing systems recover end-effector pose from monocular visual-inertial odometry, which is subject to scale ambiguity and drift, or delegate tracking to closed-source modules and external infrastructure that reintroduce cost and setup burden. We present OpenJaws, a fully open hardware and software framework for sensorized UMI that improves localization and simplifies deployment across robot platforms. OpenJaws pairs a modular, 3D-printed gripper exposing a standardized ISO adapter with a low-cost stereo camera to recover metric camera trajectories. We further introduce UMI-Loc-Bench-v1, a benchmark quantifying real-world localization accuracy for handheld data-collection devices, and show that stereo localization substantially outperforms monocular alternatives. Finally, we demonstrate that policies trained on data collected with OpenJaws can be deployed on a real robot across multiple tasks. Hardware, software, and data are released under a commercially permissive license. Code, data, and videos are available at this https URL

papers.title: REACH: An RL-based Hierarchical Humanoid Crawling Framework for Adaptable Confined Space Traversal
papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion in confined spaces requires continuous height adaptation across multiple locomotion modes, yet most existing approaches remain limited to height-adjustable bipedal walking. We present REACH, an RL-based hierarchical framework that enables a Unitree G1 humanoid to traverse height-constrained environments through variable-height bipedal walking and crawling. The learned policies regulate body height over complementary command ranges of 1.27--0.50m in bipedal locomotion and 0.50--0.20m in crawling, extending traversal beyond the clearance limits of crouched walking. To address contact-rich crawling dynamics, we employ a history-conditioned latent representation that captures terrain and interaction context from proprioceptive observations. A bidirectional transition policy further connects crouched bipedal locomotion and crawling across large kinematic and contact discontinuities. These skills are integrated with a LiDAR-based planner that converts point clouds into collision-free three-dimensional paths and locomotion commands, including proactive height targets. Real-world experiments demonstrate accurate height and velocity tracking, robust terrain traversal, reliable mode transitions and confined-space traversal with the proposed pipeline. Code and videos are available at this https URL .

papers.title: CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.abstract: Humans are dexterous, but traditional data collection paradigms such as teleoperation, kinesthetic teaching, and wearable exoskeletons force humans to act through the robot embodiment, bottlenecking their dexterity. Retargeting can avoid this. However, existing methods purely translate kinematics and ignore the real-world contact dynamics essential for task success. We present CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation, a simulator and object-free framework that retargets human demonstrations to robot actions by explicitly preserving contact force targets. CARD unifies human data sources including video, motion capture, and tactile gloves via a shared hand--contact representation and generates explicit contact force targets in addition to kinematics. To maintain these contact targets during hardware open-loop replay, CARD also introduces a tactile tracking controller. For video which does not contain an explicit tactile source, we present Vid-HACO, our video-to-contact model that sets a new state of the art. Across our video, glove, motion-capture data and the GRAB dataset, CARD maintains contact on $43$--$78\%$ of contact frames, while kinematic and object-aware retargeting methods maintain contact on $<10\%$ and $22.5\%$ of the frames respectively. Further, integrating our formulation into physics-based retargeting improves strict task success from 12\% to 32\% on GRAB dataset. Finally, we show that our tactile tracker is critical to reproduce demonstrated forces during hardware replay. These results establish that contact preservation via CARD is a scalable interface for transferring human dexterity to robots.

papers.title: A Trainable CPG Framework for Quadruped Locomotion
papers.abstract: We present CPG-ENN, a trainable quadruped locomotion framework that combines explicit neural coordination with learned motion realization. A symmetry-based eight-neuron central pattern generator (CPG) supplies gait rhythms, while a pretrained, leg-shared execution neural network (ENN) maps rhythmic signals and trajectory parameters to joint-angle references without online inverse kinematics. A single feedback policy modulates six physically interpretable trajectory variables. The controller tracks planar velocity and yaw-rate commands across walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk without gait-specific learned controllers or transitionspecific rewards. Simulation yields 99.39% transition success across all 20 directed gait pairs and all source-target speed combinations from {0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0} m/s. Ablations show high cross-gait transition feasibility without transition exposure; exposure mainly refines gait acquisition and velocity transients. Comparisons with AllGaits and Walk These Ways demonstrate accurate gait-speed regulation, and Unitree Go2 experiments validate five gaits and their transitions.

papers.title: A generalist policy for muscle-driven control across individual musculoskeletal models
papers.abstract: Differences in musculoskeletal morphology challenge policy reuse across individual models. Here we present MyoAcross, a framework that combines individual musculoskeletal model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning and virtual model augmentation to enable muscle-driven reference-motion tracking without individual fine-tuning. Across 31 held-out individual models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24% completion and reduces tracking error by 22.60% relative to an unconditioned multilayer perceptron. Policy reuse extends to models of 22 held-out individuals constructed from single-image shape estimates, measured height and body mass, and, with asymmetry augmentation, to models with unilateral lower-limb shortening. Comparisons with measurements from 120 additional individuals show agreement in vertical ground reaction force waveforms and channel-dependent agreement between simulated muscle activations and electromyography. These results establish a common control framework for comparative simulations of movement across individual musculoskeletal models.

papers.title: RoboAuto: Autonomous Robot Program Search through Multi-Level Physical Understanding
papers.abstract: Recently, LLM-based autonomous agents have shown strong capabilities in iteratively generating, evaluating, and refining executable solutions. In robotic manipulation, Code-as-Policy lets these agents search over modular and editable robot programs. However, effective program search requires physical understanding: agents must understand how objects can be manipulated, how scene geometry constrains actions, and why interactions succeed or fail. Existing methods rely mainly on execution feedback for program refinement, often leaving these physical questions unresolved. We introduce RoboAuto, a framework for robot program search that explicitly organizes physical understanding at the object, scene, and interaction levels through three components. First, a hierarchical knowledge base combines executable skills with object-centric knowledge of affordances, spatial relations, and action effects, learned from embodied data and online task solving. Second, scene grounding connects this knowledge to the current environment by identifying relevant objects and resolving action-critical quantities. Third, multi-stage planning with self-designed experiments checks whether each stage produces its expected physical effects and actively tests competing hypotheses to resolve physical uncertainties. RoboAuto achieves superior performance across five benchmark families, attaining an 89.1% success rate on short-horizon LIBERO-PRO tasks and more than twice the mean success rate of ASPIRE on LIBERO-PRO Long and LIBERO-Plus. It also outperforms ASPIRE and $\pi_{0.5}$ on three challenging long-horizon real-robot tasks requiring precise manipulation. We further show that the knowledge base transfers across simulators and embodiments, and that program search performance scales with its size. Project page: this https URL

papers.title: GRAFT: Geometry-Aware Residual Adaptation for Foundation Trackers
papers.abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) provide reusable whole-body motion priors: given a kinematic reference, they generate coordinated joint commands for motion replay, teleoperation, and VLA control. However, trained primarily on flat-ground motion, BFMs lack an explicit mechanism to adapt foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing to local terrain. Many terrain-aware BFM approaches address this limitation by retraining or fine-tuning the tracker together with perception, incurring substantial data and computation costs while coupling ordinary tracking to the perception pathway. To bridge this gap, we propose GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation framework for frozen behavior trackers. GRAFT preserves the BFM parameters and motion-reference interface, while a lightweight adapter adds terrain-conditioned corrections only to lower-body execution targets. The adapter is trained with task and foot-geometry rewards, regularized to suppress unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth. Because the frozen BFM already provides whole-body reference tracking and nominal locomotion, GRAFT reduces terrain learning to a focused execution-adaptation problem. We instantiate the framework on four frozen trackers and evaluate stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation. We further validate it through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1, where the adapted SONIC tracker traverses terrain with onboard depth and unmodified references.

papers.title: SVIn+: Multi-Modal Framework for Robust Underwater State Estimation using 3D Sonar, Visual-Inertial, Water-Pressure, and DVL
papers.abstract: As expansion and scalability in underwater oper- ations becomes more important and challenging, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) become more relevant and the necessity for reliable autonomy more critical. A fundamental challenge in any autonomous underwater operation, from control to safe navigation and mapping, is state estimation; a notorious hard problem to address, especially in low visibility conditions. In this paper, we tackle this problem, by presenting SVIn+, a multi-sensor framework for robust state estimation of AUVs equipped with an IMU, cameras, a water-pressure sensor, a Doppler Velocity Log (DVL), and a compact 3D sonar. This framework extends an established open-source state-of-the-art visual-inertial SLAM, SVIn, by integrating water-pressure and DVL measurements into a tightly-coupled nonlinear optimiza- tion formulation resulting in improved estimates. To leverage the structural information of recently available 3D acoustic sonars while maintaining computational efficiency, we introduce a hierarchical architecture that incorporates estimates from a decoupled front-end via KISS-ICP, treated as relative pose factors within the factor graph. The proposed framework is validated through field deployments in a shipwreck and coral reef, demonstrating drift mitigation and global consistency. papers.title: Whole-Body Humanoid Control via Stochastic Motion Tokenization
papers.abstract: While velocity-commanded RL policies are effective for controlling quadrupeds, they are a limited interface for humanoids that need to perform complex whole-body motions. Furthermore, RL tracking policies for whole-body motions typically have limited information about the desired future motion, preventing them from performing controlled deviations to achieve long-term task success; such information is particularly relevant when a controller must prepare for transitions between behaviors. We address these challenges using concise motion representations that can be generated by a high-level controller, given a behavior label or text command. These representations can be fed directly into a tracking policy to provide a detailed motion reference. Our method exhibits a high degree of flexibility in performing real-world robot motions such as dancing, fighting, or walking based on conditional information. At matched capacity, our adopted stochastic motion tokenizer reconstructs motions from the Unitree G1 at a level that exceeds state-of-the-art approaches such as finite scalar quantization (FSQ) and the vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-VAE). The resulting discrete interface conditions whole-body tracking policies that execute generated dance, fight, and walk motions lasting 16.8 s each and a 35 s fight-to-dance sequence on a physical Unitree G1.

papers.title: Ground Sample Distance Constrained k-Coverage Viewpoint Planning via Set Multi-Cover Formulation
papers.abstract: Drone-based 3D reconstruction and inspection require viewpoints that satisfy image-quality constraints while observing each surface region multiple times, which overlap-based planning heuristics do not guarantee. We study ground sample distance (GSD)-constrained $k$-coverage viewpoint selection for structures represented by surface voxels. Candidate viewpoints are generated along outward surface directions, screened with distance, viewing-angle, field-of-view, and occlusion tests, and augmented for voxels with insufficient visibility. Selection is then posed as set multi-cover with per-voxel coverage demands. We propose a dynamically weighted greedy heuristic that prioritizes remaining coverage deficits and scarce viewing alternatives, and compare it with sequential overlap-based pruning and an integer linear programming (ILP) formulation on the same candidate pools. Across two structures, four voxel resolutions, and three coverage requirements, the proposed approach achieves full or near-full $k$-coverage with compact viewpoint sets, using only 3.00--16.39\% more viewpoints than ILP while offering an interpretable selection process based on coverage deficits and viewpoint availability.

papers.title: A Singularity Avoiding Track Model for Race Car Optimization
papers.abstract: A track fitting pipeline is presented that converts a measured racetrack point cloud into a closed, $C^4$ differentiable, three-dimensional surface model suitable for high-fidelity Modelica race-car optimization. The surface is a Monge patch, parametrised by a curvilinear arc-length coordinate measured along the minimum-curvature line (MCL) and a signed lateral offset, with a height polynomial of user-selectable degree capturing the cross-sectional elevation profile. The choice of MCL as the reference line is deliberate since anchoring the same surface on the geometric centre-line can cause adjacent normals to cross inside the drivable region on tight corners. The resulting non-injective parametrisation assigns multiple curvilinear addresses to the same three-dimensional point and returns invalid road geometry. The MCL is obtained from a quadratic program that minimises integrated curvature subject to track-boundary, periodicity, and jerk-regularisation constraints. By reducing total curvature while remaining within the track bounds, the MCL moves the region of parametrisation breakdown outside the drivable strip on all circuits studied, keeps the normal map injective across the full track width, and yields a more linear time-to-arc-length transformation for minimum lap-time problems. The fitted surface and the associated track widths are exported as periodic piecewise-quintic $C^4$ B-splines, solved as a nonlinear program.

papers.title: A 2-DOF MultiBody Track Joint for Race Car Optimization
papers.abstract: TrackJoint is a Modelica MultiBody component that turns a three-dimensional road surface into a joint with two degrees of freedom. The two joint coordinates are the distance travelled along a reference line and the sideways offset from that line. Together they give the position, orientation and angular velocity of a single frame_b connector. All road geometry reaches the joint as a small set of periodic piecewise-quintic splines, so one component can represent any circuit whose splines have been fitted beforehand. The road constraint is closed with d'Alembert's principle. The two generalized forces that belong to the joint coordinates are set to zero, so no Lagrange multipliers are needed. The joint is connected to a multibody race car in Dymola and the pair is exported as one FMI~3.0 FMU. The same FMU is then used for time-domain simulation and for CasADi/IPOPT minimum lap-time optimization, with no change to the model in between. This works because the joint keeps the arc-length coordinate as a real state and publishes its time derivative, which is the quantity that lets the problem be rewritten with distance We report results for minimum lap time simulations on the Singapore Formula~1 circuit.

papers.title: HIDRA: Hierarchical Dual-Routing Attention for Replay-Free Lifelong Imitation Learning
papers.abstract: Robotic agents operating in real-world environments must adapt continuously from a stream of multimodal demonstrations, often under constraints that preclude storing or revisiting past data. In this replay-free, single-pass lifelong imitation learning setting, sequential updates can progressively distort the representation space, making expert-based approaches particularly sensitive to routing interference, causing expert selection to degrade over time. We propose HIDRA, a structured routing framework that mitigates this issue through a hierarchical dual-attention mechanism, which decouples instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement. To further stabilize routing under representation drift, HIDRA introduces a key-level geometric regularization that enforces both alignment within tasks and separation across tasks. The resulting approach enables reliable expert selection while supporting an expandable set of experts for continual adaptation. We evaluate HIDRA on several LIBERO benchmark suites, including more challenging variants with heterogeneous task sequences and paraphrased language instructions. Our approach consistently outperforms both replay-free and replay-based baselines, improving AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting, with stronger gains under high interference and language variation. papers.title: SG^2SLAM: Spatial Geometry-Informed 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM for Monocular Outdoor Navigation
papers.abstract: Monocular outdoor navigation requires robust camera motion estimation and a dense, navigable map, where 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM serves this task through an explicit differentiable parameterization and closed-form projection. However, typically, the geometry is recovered by associating 2D pixels with 3D points, so a modular SLAM system absorbs tracking error into the map, leading to cascading degradation. To address these gaps, we present SG^2SLAM, which couples streaming spatial geometry with a ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel. Streaming spatial geometry replaces the per- frame cross-dimensional correspondence with a chunk-level metric prior that supervises tracking and mapping from one source. A ray-conditioned kernel extends each primitive with a viewing-direction subspace that senses the monocular camera viewpoints. The joint optimization over spatial geometry and poses ensures a globally consistent map and trajectory outcome. Experiments on the KITTI and Waymo Open datasets show that our SG^2SLAM surpasses the per-frame association baselines in the monocular outdoor navigation task. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

papers.title: ASPEN: Adaptive Semantic Reasoning via Command Persistence Prediction for Efficient Navigation VLAs
papers.abstract: Navigation vision-language-action (VLA) policies repeatedly invoke costly semantic reasoning even when the next command remains unchanged. Command reuse can reduce computation but risks missing instruction-dependent turns or stops. We introduce ASPEN, an event-triggered scheduler based on command persistence prediction: estimating whether the frozen base policy would reissue its previous command. A lightweight multimodal predictor combines temporal observations, language instructions, execution history, and cached VLA confidence. At eligible command boundaries, sufficient predicted persistence permits command reuse. Otherwise, ASPEN triggers fresh semantic reasoning from the VLA. Evaluated with frozen NaVILA on cross-dataset RxR-CE val-unseen, ASPEN reduces VLA calls by 9.5% and estimated inference time by 8.1%, including scheduling overhead. It maintains comparable navigation performance and preserves identical baseline action sequences on 92.1% of episodes.

papers.title: Learning Multi-Phase Robot Loco-Manipulation via Phase-Conditioned Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Complex whole-body loco-manipulation requires executing diverse maneuvers, such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion, within a single long-horizon task. While performing simple pick-and-place behaviors is well-established, scaling to complex, long-horizon tasks remains difficult. Currently, this challenge is addressed by relying on human motion data and correspondingly humanoid platforms, which limits platform independence and introduces substantial data processing overhead. Instead, we extend proximal policy optimization (PPO) to train a single policy for multi-phase tasks across diverse robotic hardware, leveraging prior task structure to shape behavior. Our method adapts PPO using a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated reward functions, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to guide exploration. To support varied hardware, we employ a decoupled hierarchical control architecture that separates lower-level balancing dynamics from high-level phase execution. We demonstrate multi-stage loco-manipulation skills on hardware on both the Unitree G1 and a Boston Dynamics Spot equipped with a manipulator arm, and validate our design choices through ablations. Our approach enables the acquisition of complex loco-manipulation behaviors purely through environment interaction while directly incorporating high-level task structure into policy learning.

papers.title: cuArms: GPU-Accelerated Conflict-Based Planning for Multi-Arm Manipulation
papers.abstract: Multi-arm manipulation has the potential to dramatically improve the throughput, efficiency, and dexterity of many manipulation tasks. Recent work coordinates multiple robot arms in a shared workcell by allocating and scheduling tasks for greater parallelism, jointly planning multi-arm motions, or directly learning multi-arm policies. So far, these approaches are either too slow, rely on domain-specific assumptions, or scale poorly with the number of robots and task horizon. Thus, we introduce cuArms, a conflict-based planner co-designed with GPU parallelism that efficiently decomposes the search space using reusable multi-modal roadmaps for individual robots and resolves conflicts and deadlocks through a lazy search. To jointly optimize task assignment, schedules, motions, and manipulation skills, we integrate a high-level scheduler that proposes candidate skeletons for cuArms to ground into coordinated manipulation plans. Experimental results show that our method establishes a new state of the art, with real-time initial solutions and anytime improvements in both motion quality and scheduling, without days of domain-specific training required by learning approaches. Videos of both simulated and real-world industrial tasks are available on this https URL .

papers.title: Program-Level Adversarial Co-Adaptive Self-Play for Robotic Security
papers.abstract: Coding agents can adapt robotic software by revising executable programs, but successful responses to an evolving opponent may not remain effective. We present a framework for program-level adversarial co-adaptive self-play in which coding agents generate attacks and defenses from tested opponent code and mission feedback, without model fine-tuning. Environment-specific interfaces support external programs for autonomous driving and SDK-level defenses for humanoid locomotion. Two eight-generation case studies reveal concrete software responses: a driving defender introduces direct-actuation recovery, while a humanoid defender revises incoming-state validation. These responses provide local task recovery but do not establish sustained robustness. The framework makes such adaptation and limitations observable through executable artifacts and task-level evidence.

papers.title: Closed-Loop Aware Planning via Imitation-Free Speed Scoring for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has predominantly relied on open-loop imitation learning for training, which presents two limitations. First, expert demonstrations show only one behavior per scenario, so the model cannot learn alternative valid behaviors and, in turn, cannot adapt to user-specified preferences at test time. Second, noise or ambiguity in these demonstrations can produce inconsistent, unreliable supervision for the end-to-end models. Driving is inherently multi-modal: multiple different behaviors can be valid responses to the same scene, and this diversity arises largely from speed rather than path. We introduce a planning paradigm that learns the path through imitation while scoring a set of candidate speeds across multiple criteria with a learned function supervised by physically grounded safety constraints. We realize this paradigm as Closed-Loop Aware Planning for Autonomous Driving (CLAP-AD), a plug-in planning head that integrates with existing end-to-end driving models and, to our knowledge, is the first to enable explicit test-time control over their speed selection without speed-conditioned training. On Bench2Drive-Speed, CLAP-AD sets a new state of the art Speed-Adherence Score of 82.53, topping TFv6, the strongest baseline on this metric, by 12.9 points while retaining strong closed-loop driving performance. On Bench2Drive, it improves driving score by +28.5 and +32.7 over UniAD and VAD, and on NAVSIM v2, built on real-world driving data, EPDMS by +6.1 over its backbone. Project page: this https URL

papers.title: Rollback: Experience Backtracking in World Models for Policy Improvement
papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models offer a scalable alternative to costly real-world interaction for improving robot policies. However, existing world-model-based methods largely treat world models as forward-only surrogates of the physical environment, leaving untapped a capability no physical environment affords: rewinding to past decision points to explore counterfactual futures. We introduce Rollback, a policy improvement paradigm that turns world models from passive simulators into counterfactual engines: it rolls back to critical decision points, branches into alternative actions, and contrasts their outcomes to attribute success to individual decisions. This concentrates imagination where it matters most and distills counterfactual outcomes into fine-grained, action-level supervision without a separately learned value model. We build a scalable training system that unifies distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution, forming a self-reinforcing cycle: real-world experience continually sharpens the world model, and a sharper world model in turn drives further policy improvement. We term the world-model side of this cycle test-time physics grounding, a capability that hand-built physics simulators lack: while the world model serves as the training environment, real transitions from the policy it trains correct its dynamics through a lightweight LoRA pipeline. Experiments on three challenging real-world tasks show that Rollback improves success rates over the strongest baseline by an absolute 10.67%, 11.11%, and 11.85% on block extraction, ball tossing, and tabletop curling, respectively, while achieving more stable improvement throughout training. Although initialized from teleoperated demonstrations far below human level, Rollback surpasses the average success rate of human players on both ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours of training.

papers.title: E0.5: From Reconstructive to Future-Predictive 3D Foundations for Robotic World-Action Modeling
papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) offer a promising framework for embodied intelligence, yet mainstream approaches remain centered on video foundation models or vision-language models. Even when geometric features extracted by 3D models such as VGGT are incorporated, they are typically passed into a video model or VLM that serves as the primary backbone, leaving 3D geometry as an auxiliary input or prediction target rather than the native foundation for world modeling. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. E0.5 introduces two key innovations. First, it adopts a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone, making 3D geometry the native representation for both world modeling and action prediction. Second, it explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions, enabling the model to capture geometric world dynamics beyond action-only modeling or future video prediction. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 first demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5 without embodied-data pretraining, achieving success rates of 89.90\% and 50.09\% under clean and randomized settings, respectively. Building on these results, we further pretrain E0.5 on more than 160k robot trajectories from AgiBotWorld-Beta, jointly learning robot actions and future geometry within the pretrained 3D foundation. This embodied pretraining improves mean real-world manipulation success rates by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of geometry-native foundations to acquire robot interaction knowledge and transfer it to physical manipulation. E0.5 embodies this geometry-native approach as a member of the VWA family of world-action models.

papers.title: Perceiving and Predicting Dynamic Sports: Spatiotemporal Intelligence in Vision Models for Egocentric Tennis Video
papers.abstract: Agile robots require spatiotemporal intelligence to interpret scenes, reason about interactions, and anticipate future events. Yet it remains unclear how well foundation vision models support these capabilities, particularly from a moving egocentric camera, which is a natural view for robots. To investigate this, we collect an annotated tennis dataset and train a suite of vision models on spatiotemporal tasks. Our dataset contains egocentric video synchronized with five allocentric videos, estimated global positions, labeled contact times, and annotated stroke types. We then evaluate seven prediction tasks from egocentric images: 2D ego player and 3D ball localization, future player and ball trajectories, forehand or backhand stroke anticipation, time to the next ego player ball contact, and 3D ball position at that contact. We compare image encoders, video encoders, and vision-language models with jointly trained prediction heads. The best performing models achieve mean current-frame localization errors of 0.14 m for the ego player and 0.54 m for the ball, future forecasting errors of 0.34 m for the ego player and 0.91 m for the ball over 1.1 s, and a mean contact-time prediction error of 0.14 s. Auxiliary depth information substantially improves 3D ball localization, suggesting that inferring metric depth remains a challenge. Longer image histories do not improve ball forecasting, indicating that representations exploit scene context rather than rely solely on inter-frame motion. Finally, we propose a conditional diffusion model to generate whole-body kinematic tennis motion from vision encoder predictions on egocentric video at real-time rates, adapting movements as predictions are refined. These results move towards a deeper understanding of how foundation vision models can support real-time dynamic robots using egocentric video.

papers.title: Understanding Human-Robot Collaboration through Joint Action
papers.abstract: Human-robot collaboration requires partners to coordinate interdependent contributions toward a shared goal. Joint Action theory provides concepts for understanding this coordination, but how these concepts are instantiated and combined across empirical research remains fragmented. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA 2020, identifying 83 empirical papers published between 2021 and 2026. Through theory-driven framework analysis, we organized the literature into nine constructs across three capacities: Representation, Prediction, and Integration. We analyze how these constructs are distributed and co-occur across studies, revealing where empirical evidence concentrates and where it is absent. By mapping empirical HRC research onto a unified Joint Action framework, this review offers a coherent overview of HRC studies, identifies gaps in current evidence, and provides guidelines for future research.

papers.title: Vision-Language-Action or World-Action? Just Action Models
papers.abstract: The vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action model (WAM) communities debate whether control policies should inherit pretrained knowledge from vision-language models or from visual generators. The debate, however, bundles three separable choices: backbone initialization, the objective applied to future observations, and whether the machinery for that future loss is kept at inference. A gap between a VLA and a WAM therefore cannot simply be attributed to any one of them. We show that decoupling these choices yields a common framework for both families, which we term Just Action Model (JAM): a pretrained visual backbone with an action expert, trained with an action loss and a foresight loss. The foresight loss trains current-observation features to predict frozen encodings of the recorded future through a prediction head discarded after training, so no visual generation is involved in either training or inference, and the backbone can be chosen freely. We first compare objectives within fixed policy architectures, then evaluate the foresight recipe across backbone families. The resulting JAM policies outperform their matched FastWAM and ImageWAM counterparts on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and achieve similar or slightly higher success rates on RoboTwin. Compared with FastWAM, JAM improves the success rates from 97.0%/55.3%/91.2% to 98.2%/64.5%/91.4%, respectively. With cached foresight targets, JAM reduces estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by 73% relative to FastWAM. Our results show that future supervision improves control without visual generation or additional inference machinery, and strong foresight performance is attainable with either generator-initialized or vision-language backbones. papers.title: FastBEVFusion: Simple Multi-Modal Fusion for 3D Object Detection at 50 FPS
papers.abstract: Reliable real-time 3D object detection based on LiDAR and camera data is critical for safety in autonomous driving, where systems must accurately perceive their surroundings with minimal latency. Many state-of-the-art systems achieve high-quality detection results but fail to meet real-time constraints, limiting their practical use. To address this challenge, we propose FastBEVFusion, a simple, fast, and robust fusion system for 3D object detection. Based on modality-specific features, FastBEVFusion projects these features into semi-aligned modality-specific BEV spaces, without relying on a computationally intensive and potentially error-prone depth estimation. Given these BEV spaces, we propose a light-weight, soft, and dynamic fusion module based on cross-attention, which adapts dynamically to the scene context and enables feature fusion across the entire BEV spaces. Experiments on the complex nuScenes dataset show that FastBEVFusion outperforms state-of-the-art real-time systems, and achieves over 50 FPS without deployment libraries. Additionally, our system shows strong robustness to calibration errors, making FastBEVFusion a powerful 3D object detection system for real-world applications.

papers.title: MCP-Net: Real-Time Coronary Perception Network and Topological Analysis for Robotic Guidewire Navigation
papers.abstract: Coronary guidewire navigation during percutaneous coronary intervention requires continuous interpretation of vessel anatomy, guidewire position, and target stenosis under two-dimensional X-ray fluoroscopy. While existing approaches commonly address vessel segmentation or device localization as separate tasks, a robotic system requires a more structured perception of the coronary scene to support downstream navigation. In this work, we present a simulation-driven framework centered on a Multi-Task Coronary Perception Network (MCP-Net) for robotic guidewire navigation, integrating coronary vessel segmentation, vascular topology extraction, and roadmap generation. Starting from three-dimensional coronary CT angiography, we generate simulated fluoroscopy images containing vascular structures, simulated guidewires, stenotic lesions with varying severity, and diverse vascular geometries, together with simulation-derived ground truth. MCP-Net jointly performs coronary vessel segmentation, guidewire-tip localization, and stenosis localization from a single fluoroscopic frame. These predictions are subsequently converted into a structured vascular graph containing centerlines, bifurcations, endpoints, branch directions, and branch angles. By associating the predicted stenosis with this graph, the framework generates a roadmap from the automatically selected graph root toward the target lesion. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework can jointly recover coronary perception targets and transform them into an interpretable vascular representation suitable for downstream robotic navigation.

papers.title: Polarity--Time Interaction and Multi-Level Reliability for Event-Based Spacecraft Pose Estimation
papers.abstract: Sparse event responses produce uneven keypoint errors whose effects on spacecraft pose depend on correspondence geometry and the reliability of successive observations. We present a reliability-aware framework connecting polarity--time localization, geometric recovery, event--CAD refinement, and trajectory optimization. A three-branch representation combines positive events, negative events, and recent-event timing through cross-branch attention and gating, followed by spatiotemporal aggregation. An ordered semantic-point head estimates relative correspondence precision for geometrically constrained pose recovery. Event-edge and CAD-projection agreement then guide local pose refinement under keypoint-geometry safeguards. At the sequence level, a ten-dimensional descriptor combines heatmap shape, reprojection consistency, and geometric conditioning to set time-aligned observation scales. On the official SPADES challenge test set, the complete system achieves a combined pose score of 0.0474, approximately 5.4\% below PASAN+IRIS. Validation ablations reduce the score from 0.0772 for base localization with uniform PnP to 0.0514 for the complete cascade; on identical single-frame observations, quality weighting reduces the score from 0.0549 with constant-weight optimization to 0.0514.

papers.title: Bridging Exploration and Loss of Plasticity in On-Policy Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have been observed to lose the ability to adaptively learn from new data, a phenomenon termed Loss of Plasticity (LoP). While many metrics have been shown to correlate with it, the causal mechanisms and the geometric conditions from which it can arise have not been clearly identified. We analyze LoP in Proximal Policy Optimization with isotropic Gaussian policies, the state-of-the-art formulation for many continuous action spaces in RL. We report multiple metrics which characterize the effect that the policy standard deviation $\sigma$ has on LoP, and we also suggest related explanations for the effectiveness of widely adopted LoP mitigation techniques. We observe a significant effect of $\sigma$ on the extent of LoP, and accompany this with both theoretical and experimental supporting arguments. Our experimental validation consists of LoP benchmark evaluations against standard baselines as well as real-world policy deployment on a 7-DoF robotic arm.

papers.title: Compatibility and future-proof testing for multi-agent systems
papers.abstract: Independently developed autonomous agents, such as autonomous vehicles, must guarantee joint compatibility, such as safety and task-completion requirements, when they operate in a shared environment. Existing methods require a centrally designed specification, or interaction mechanism before any agent is deployed. However, such centralized design is unrealistic when agent designs are confidential to their developers, and it is not flexible enough to accommodate future agent designs. We study a bi-level structure in which a regulator coordinates developers by publishing seed agents, and each developer independently tests its agent to ensure that it is compatible with every seed-compatible agent, a property we call future-proofness. Under this structure, joint compatibility is guaranteed for any agents that are designed and tested independently, without any coordination with each other. In this work, we first formulate compatibility for general multi-agent systems and show why it is not trivially implied by seed-compatibility. We then characterize the future-proof agents as the closure of the seed and show that this closure is monotone in the seed. Finally, we study a class of executable tests that involve interaction with the seed alone, and we ask to what extent such tests can distinguish the future-proof agents.

papers.title: Calibrated for Which Policy? Conformal Uncertainty for Fixed World Models Under Intervention
papers.abstract: Changing a deployment policy can invalidate a world model's uncertainty while leaving the physical transition mechanism and predictor unchanged. For one-step prediction, if source and target laws share the conditional mechanism $P(Y|X)=Q(Y|X)$, then the intervention is identified by the pre-outcome change of measure $w(X)=dQ_X/dP_X$. For policy-controlled dynamics this ratio factors into state-occupancy and action-propensity terms. Weighted conformal calibration transports marginal coverage to the target law; with an estimated ratio $\hat w$, $P_Q\{Y \in C_{\hat w}(X)\} \ge 1-\alpha-TV(Q,\hat Q) \ge 1-\alpha-E_P|w-\hat w|$. Population log-loss regret for a source-versus-target domain classifier bounds the same ratio error. If $h$ is its clipped target posterior, $\rho$ is the target-domain prior, and $\Delta(h)$ is population log-loss regret, then $E_P|w-\hat w_h| \le (1/(\rho\gamma))\sqrt{\Delta(h)/2}$. An exact cancellation improves the dependence from a generic odds-map bound of order $\gamma^{-2}$ to $(\rho\gamma)^{-1}$. Our experiments use a released DINO-feature world model and physical Franka trajectories. Under the strongest controlled state-action shift, ordinary 90% conformal sets cover 55.0%, whereas oracle and learned-ratio calibration cover 91.0% and 90.9%. The learned surrogate remains within 0.9% total variation of the target law. Calibration is relative to the deployment law: the model can remain fixed while calibration follows the intervention. We machine-check in Lean 4 the finite-support algebraic and causal identities used in the classifier-regret argument, including its coverage-composition step.

executive_summary: Several works advance complex robot coordination and contact-rich manipulation: cuArms introduces a GPU-parallel, conflict-based planner with reusable multi-modal roadmaps and lazy conflict resolution plus high-level scheduling, reporting real-time initial solutions and anytime refinements that outperform prior multi-arm task allocation and coordination methods on simulated and real industrial tasks; an extended PPO framework with phase-conditioned critics, phase-gated rewards, a multi-phase reset curriculum, and hierarchical control learns a single loco-manipulation policy that executes multi-stage behaviors on both Unitree G1 and Boston Dynamics Spot hardware without human motion data; a contact-planning method for bimanual non-prehensile tilting uses signed friction distance to derive task-adaptive friction margins within sequential SOCPs, improving robustness to object variations compared with fixed or no margins in simulation and hardware; and a sanding-focused study of lightweight mobile manipulators shows that low base–ground resistance yields only 54–70% of a commanded 100 N contact force and up to 100 mm tool error, arguing that joint consideration of force, motion, and vibration is needed to characterize non-rigid bases under contact.

Multiple humanoid control and motion-generation frameworks target scalable whole-body skills: a stochastic motion tokenizer conditions tracking policies on discrete motion tokens from behavior labels or text, outperforming FSQ and VQ-VAE in G1 motion reconstruction while enabling 16.8 s dance/fight/walk clips and a 35 s fight-to-dance sequence on hardware; GRAFT adds a lightweight, terrain-aware residual adapter on top of frozen humanoid behavior foundation models, using depth-based terrain cues and regularization to enable simulated stair/gap/platform locomotion and real-world uneven-terrain traversal on Unitree G1 without retraining the base tracker; REACH combines RL-based bipedal and crawling policies with a LiDAR planner so a G1 can track body heights from 1.27–0.50 m (bipedal) and 0.50–0.20 m (crawling) for confined-space navigation with robust mode transitions; and HumiTransfer converts in-the-wild human–human interaction videos into physically plausible human–humanoid interactions, producing the ~500k-frame HumiMimic dataset for Unitree R1 Edu and HighTorque Mini-hi and demonstrating improved motion fidelity and real-robot execution of partner-following behaviors over baselines.

Several works focus on dexterous manipulation interfaces, retargeting, and hardware: CARD unifies video, motion capture, and tactile glove data via an object-free contact-anchored hand representation, preserving contact in 43–78% of frames (vs <10% and 22.5% for purely kinematic and object-aware baselines) and raising strict task success on GRAB from 12% to 32% when integrated into physics-based retargeting, with hardware tests showing its tactile tracker is needed to reproduce contact forces; a LEAP-hand training recipe with diverse resets, goal generation from grasp datasets, and an adaptive friction curriculum plus a tunable residual safety filter yields zero-shot sim-to-real in-hand pose reaching with 95.2% goal success within 2 cm/0.4 rad (91.5% with safety filtering) over 13.3 hours and 4,800 unseen goals while reducing object drops by 75%; EgoThumb offers a lightweight supernumerary robotic thumb with forearm-mounted actuation and an egocentric visual imitation policy that maps palm-camera images to joint positions for autonomous grasp/hold assistance that generalizes across users and environments; Torch-Hand introduces a 21-DoF anthropomorphic hand with palm-integrated screw-linkage actuation and decoupled DoFs, experimentally validated for workspace, thumb opposition, 33-grasp coverage, grasp force, payload, and task-level manipulation; and ActiveAlign’s Real-to-Sim-to-Real alignment—via ActiveAlign-Waving for hand–eye calibration and ActiveAlign-Touching for tactile object pose refinement—supports curating uncalibrated datasets and enables millimeter-scale tasks such as button pressing and slider manipulation on a Unitree G1.

Perception, odometry, and navigation for mobile robots are advanced through several frameworks: RESPLE2 models 6-DoF motion with non-uniform B-splines in an iterated EKF with inertial-informed control-point prediction, motion-adaptive knot placement, and continuous-time fusion of LiDAR, cameras, IMUs, and leg kinematics, achieving real-time, competitive-or-better accuracy and robustness on handheld, tracked, legged, and aerial-legged platforms, especially in aggressive maneuvers; Omni-IGN uses quad-fisheye RGB, an attention-based RL policy, and a collision-aware safety layer for fully onboard image-goal drone navigation, outperforming continuous-action baselines on Habitat ImageNav, improving collision avoidance with learned depth in IsaacSim, and transferring zero-shot to real drones without external localization; RAVEN unifies frontier and loop-closure planning for quadrotor active SLAM using a utility vector to trade off exploration vs localization and a perception-aware planner that minimizes visual estimation error, outperforming existing active SLAM baselines and running fully onboard in challenging field environments; and VLA-Stem wraps vision-language-action policies with a learned execution-level safety layer that converts action chunks into motion references and RL-trained trajectory adjustments, roughly doubling constrained-scenario collision-free success (52.8% vs 23.7% for the strongest baseline) in simulation and reducing collisions in real robots while preserving unconstrained performance.

New datasets and theoretical structures support embodied intelligence research: an egocentric tennis dataset with synchronized ego/allocentric views, 3D positions, and annotated strokes enables seven spatiotemporal prediction tasks where foundation models achieve 0.14 m ego-player and 0.54 m ball localization error, 0.34/0.91 m future trajectory error over 1.1 s, and 0.14 s time-to-contact error, with analyses indicating that added image history does not aid ball forecasting and that auxiliary depth helps but leaves 3D ball localization challenging; and a formal study of a bi-level regulatory regime where a regulator publishes seed agents defines “future-proof” compatibility as the closure of the seed set, proves this closure is monotone in the seed, and examines executable tests that rely only on seed interactions to distinguish future-proof from non-future-proof agents within a general multi-agent compatibility framework.

institution_matches.title: cuArms: GPU-Accelerated Conflict-Based Planning for Multi-Arm Manipulation
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes cuArms, a conflict-based multi-arm manipulation planner co-designed with GPU parallelism that decomposes search using reusable multi-modal roadmaps for individual robots and resolves conflicts and deadlocks via a lazy search, integrated with a high-level scheduler that jointly optimizes task assignment, schedules, motions, and manipulation skills. In experiments on simulated and real-world industrial tasks, cuArms achieves real-time initial solutions with anytime improvements in motion quality and scheduling, establishing a new state of the art compared to prior task-allocation, joint motion-planning, and learning-based multi-arm coordination methods that can require days of domain-specific training.

institution_matches.title: Learning Multi-Phase Robot Loco-Manipulation via Phase-Conditioned Policy Optimization
institution_matches.overview: The paper extends proximal policy optimization (PPO) to multi-phase loco-manipulation by introducing a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated reward functions, and a multi-phase reset curriculum, combined with a decoupled hierarchical control architecture that separates low-level balancing from high-level phase execution to support diverse robot hardware. Using only environment interaction and no human motion data, the proposed method trains a single policy that executes complex multi-stage loco-manipulation skills on hardware for both the Unitree G1 humanoid and a Boston Dynamics Spot with a manipulator arm, with ablations validating the contributions of the phase-conditioning and curriculum design.

institution_matches.title: CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces CARD, a simulator and object-free contact-anchored retargeting framework that unifies human data sources (video, motion capture, tactile gloves) via a shared hand–contact representation to generate both kinematic trajectories and explicit contact force targets for dexterous robot manipulation, including a tactile tracking controller for hardware open-loop replay and a video-to-contact model (Vid-HACO). Across video, glove, motion-capture data, and the GRAB dataset, CARD preserves contact on 43–78% of contact frames, whereas purely kinematic and object-aware retargeting methods maintain contact on less than 10% and 22.5% of frames respectively, and integrating CARD into physics-based retargeting increases strict task success on GRAB from 12% to 32%. Hardware experiments show that the proposed tactile tracker is necessary to reproduce demonstrated contact forces during replay, supporting the claim that explicit contact preservation via CARD is an effective interface for transferring human dexterity to robots.

institution_matches.title: ActiveAlign: Aligning Egocentric Manipulation via Active Perception
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes ActiveAlign, a Real-to-Sim-to-Real alignment framework that uses active perception via two modules: ActiveAlign-Waving for hand-eye calibration through deliberate hand motions and differentiable rendering, and ActiveAlign-Touching for refining object alignment using tactile feedback to achieve millimeter-level accuracy. ActiveAlign-Waving is shown to curate simulation environments for open-sourced, uncalibrated robot manipulation datasets, and real-robot experiments on a Unitree G1 demonstrate that ActiveAlign enables fine manipulation of millimeter-scale objects, such as pressing buttons and moving sliders, by improving real2sim alignment.

institution_matches.title: Pushing Dexterity and Safety for In-Hand Object Pose Reaching That Works Remarkably Well
institution_matches.overview: The paper presents a training recipe for in-hand object pose reaching with a LEAP hand in simulation, using diverse resets and goal generation from grasp datasets and an adaptive friction curriculum, and augments the learned task policy with a learned residual safety filter whose conservativeness can be tuned to trade off performance and safety. With system identification and either motion capture or a single wrist-mounted depth camera, the learned policies transfer zero-shot to a real LEAP hand; over 13.3 hours of real-robot evaluation on 4 objects and 4,800 unseen goals, the state-based policy reaches 95.2% of goals within 2 cm and 0.4 rad, and the safety filter reduces object drops by 75% while still reaching 91.5% of goals. The resulting in-hand manipulation policies exhibit robustness to out-of-distribution goals, fast arm motions, and perturbations, and can perform tasks such as spinning a lightbulb in arbitrary poses using only a wrist camera, illustrating portability of the learned dexterous skill.

institution_matches.title: EgoThumb: A Vision-Driven Supernumerary Robotic Thumb for Autonomous Grasp and Holding Assistance
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces EgoThumb, an open-source supernumerary robotic thumb system with a compact dual tendon-driven finger whose actuation is relocated to the forearm, reducing distal weight while allowing precise active joint control for assisting hold-and-manipulate tasks. EgoThumb employs a visual imitation learning policy that maps egocentric images from a palm-facing camera directly to continuous joint positions, enabling autonomous grasp and holding assistance that infers user intent from visual context and generalizes across different users and environments.

institution_matches.title: RESPLE2: Inertial-Informed Recursive Non-Uniform Spline Estimation for Multi-Sensor Odometry with Global Refinement
institution_matches.overview: The paper presents RESPLE2, a recursive multi-sensor odometry framework that represents 6-DoF motion with non-uniform B-splines and uses knot-clamping properties to derive an inertial-informed control-point prediction within an iterated extended Kalman filter, with motion-adaptive knot placement and a reset step to maintain trajectory consistency. RESPLE2 incorporates heterogeneous sensor measurements (LiDAR, cameras, IMUs, leg kinematics) at native timestamps through continuous-time observation models, and includes a lightweight global optimization module that refines spline control points using LiDAR-visual loop-closure constraints. Across public and experimental datasets on handheld, tracked, legged, and hybrid aerial-legged platforms undergoing highly dynamic maneuvers, RESPLE2 achieves competitive or superior accuracy and robustness relative to state-of-the-art multi-sensor odometry systems under corresponding sensor configurations, while maintaining real-time performance, particularly in aggressive motions.

institution_matches.title: Perceiving and Predicting Dynamic Sports: Spatiotemporal Intelligence in Vision Models for Egocentric Tennis Video
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces an egocentric tennis dataset with synchronized egocentric and five allocentric videos, estimated global positions, labeled contact times, and annotated stroke types, and uses it to train and evaluate foundation vision models on seven spatiotemporal prediction tasks including 2D ego player and 3D ball localization, future trajectories, stroke anticipation, and contact-time and position prediction. On these tasks, the best models achieve mean current-frame localization errors of 0.14 m for the ego player and 0.54 m for the ball, future forecasting errors of 0.34 m for the ego player and 0.91 m for the ball over 1.1 s, and a mean prediction error of 0.14 s for time to next ball contact, while auxiliary depth significantly improves 3D ball localization, indicating metric depth inference remains challenging. Analysis shows that extending image history length does not improve ball forecasting, suggesting that foundation models leverage scene context rather than solely inter-frame motion, and a proposed conditional diffusion model can generate whole-body tennis motion from egocentric video at real-time rates, adapting movements as vision-based predictions are refined.

institution_matches.title: Compatibility and future-proof testing for multi-agent systems
institution_matches.overview: The paper studies a bi-level regulatory structure for multi-agent systems in which a regulator publishes seed agents and developers independently test their agents for compatibility against these seeds, defining a notion of future-proofness where any seed-compatible agents are guaranteed to be mutually compatible without direct coordination. Within a general formulation of multi-agent compatibility, the authors characterize future-proof agents as the closure of the seed set and prove that this closure is monotone in the seed, then analyze a class of executable tests that rely only on interaction with the seed to assess how effectively such tests can distinguish future-proof agents from non-future-proof ones.

institution_matches.title: Electric-Field Induction Motor with Discrete Circuit Elements and Improved Rotor Dynamics
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes an electric-field induction motor design whose rotor surface is constructed from discrete circuit elements between a finite number of conductive vanes, enabling rotor properties such as resistivity, permittivity, and circuitry to be tailored beyond what is possible with single continuum materials. Inspired by deep-bar rotors in magnetic-field induction motors, the authors design and demonstrate a macro-scale electric-field induction motor whose rotor circuitry emulates the deep-bar effect, thereby improving torque over a wide range of operating speeds by exploiting frequency-dependent rotor dynamics.

topic_matches.title: Whole-Body Humanoid Control via Stochastic Motion Tokenization
topic_matches.institution: German Research Center for AI (DFKI); Robotics Institute Germany (RIG); Technical University of Darmstadt; hessian.AI
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes a whole-body humanoid control framework that uses a stochastic motion tokenizer to produce concise motion representations, conditioned on behavior labels or text commands, which are fed as detailed motion references into a tracking policy. In motion reconstruction for the Unitree G1, the adopted stochastic motion tokenizer achieves higher reconstruction quality than finite scalar quantization (FSQ) and vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-VAE) at matched capacity. Using the discrete motion-token interface, the system conditions whole-body tracking policies that execute generated dance, fight, and walk motions of 16.8 s each and a 35 s fight-to-dance sequence on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid robot.

topic_matches.title: GRAFT: Geometry-Aware Residual Adaptation for Foundation Trackers
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation framework that leaves a humanoid behavior foundation model (BFM) frozen while a lightweight adapter adds terrain-conditioned corrections to lower-body execution targets based on task and foot-geometry rewards. GRAFT is trained by distilling privileged terrain observations into onboard depth sensing and is regularized to suppress unnecessary corrections on flat ground, treating terrain adaptation as an execution-level residual problem rather than retraining the full tracker. Instantiated on four frozen humanoid trackers, GRAFT enables locomotion over stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation and allows a Unitree G1 with the adapted SONIC tracker to traverse real-world terrain using onboard depth and unmodified motion references.

topic_matches.title: REACH: An RL-based Hierarchical Humanoid Crawling Framework for Adaptable Confined Space Traversal
topic_matches.institution: Chinese University of Hong Kong; Southern University of Science and Technology
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents REACH, an RL-based hierarchical framework that combines variable-height bipedal walking and crawling policies for a Unitree G1 humanoid to traverse height-constrained environments. The learned locomotion policies regulate body height over 1.27–0.50 m in bipedal mode and 0.50–0.20 m in crawling mode, extending traversal beyond the clearance limits of crouched walking, with a history-conditioned latent representation to handle contact-rich crawling dynamics. Integrated with a LiDAR-based planner that generates collision-free 3D paths and proactive height targets, REACH achieves accurate height and velocity tracking, robust terrain traversal, and reliable mode transitions for confined-space traversal in real-world experiments.

topic_matches.title: Mimetic Embodiment Transfer of Human-Humanoid Interaction from In-the-Wild Videos
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes HumiTransfer, a mimetic embodiment transfer framework that converts in-the-wild human–human interaction videos into physically plausible human–humanoid interactions by reconstructing 3D human motion with consistent contacts and retargeting one participant to a target humanoid using interaction-focused modeling and post-optimization for balance, contact, and collision avoidance. Applying HumiTransfer to 1,200 in-the-wild videos yields the HumiMimic dataset with about 500,000 frames of diverse interactions for the 26-DoF Unitree R1 Edu and 23-DoF HighTorque Mini-hi humanoid robots, where HumiTransfer outperforms baselines in motion fidelity, preservation of inter-body relationships, and contact accuracy. The paper demonstrates that HumiMimic supports motion generation methods for interactive humanoid behaviors that follow a human partner and that the transferred motions are physically executable on real humanoid robots.

topic_matches.title: On Shaky Ground: Characterising Non-Rigid Base Effects in Mobile Manipulation
topic_matches.institution: Australian Cobotics Centre; Faculty of Engineering; Queensland University of Technology
topic_matches.overview: The paper investigates non-rigid base effects in lightweight mobile robot manipulators via a sanding case study combining simulation and experiments on two unactuated wheeled testbeds, jointly measuring contact force, tool motion, and base vibration during sustained contact. Under low base–ground resistance, the experiments show that only 54–70% of a commanded 100 N contact force is realized and tool-center-point errors can reach 100 mm, while increasing base–ground resistance improves force realization and halts further tool displacement. The study finds that base vibration does not vary consistently with force-tracking error in the tested conditions and argues that characterizing lightweight mobile manipulation under contact should jointly consider force, motion, and vibration to understand non-rigid base behavior.

topic_matches.title: A fully articulated humanoid dexterous hand with human-level joint structure enabled by linkage-based actuation
topic_matches.institution: Robotics Institute of Zhejiang University; Zhejiang University
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents Torch-Hand, a fully articulated humanoid dexterous hand with 21 DoF that replicates the human hand’s joint structure and motion hierarchy, including a five-DoF thumb with multi-axis CMC motion and four DoF in each remaining finger. Torch-Hand employs a fully linkage-based transmission with screw-linkage actuation and all actuators integrated in the palm in a serial-robot-like configuration, yielding a compact anthropomorphic form, high grasping force and payload capacity, and a direct mapping between motor motion and joint kinematics with mechanically decoupled functional DoFs. Experimental evaluations of Torch-Hand’s workspace, fingertip coordination, thumb opposition, 33-grasp taxonomy coverage, grasping force, payload capacity, and task-level manipulation indicate that the design provides a robust hardware platform for dexterous embodied manipulation.

topic_matches.title: Keeping Contact: Task-Adaptive Friction Margins for Bimanual Non-Prehensile Manipulation
topic_matches.institution: Nanyang Technological University (NTU); R3 Institute (R3I) Singapore
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces a contact-planning method for bimanual non-prehensile manipulation that uses signed friction distance as a quantitative measure of friction margin in force space and derives task-adaptive margins based on the force correction needed to balance pivot moment deviations during tilting. These task-adaptive friction margins are incorporated into a sequence of second-order cone programs that compute globally optimal contact forces at each tilt angle, balancing the object about an environmental pivot while keeping robot and pivot contacts away from nominal friction boundaries. Simulation and real-world experiments on bimanual tilting show that the proposed planner successfully executes tasks under variations in object properties and model mismatch, and that fixed-margin or no-margin strategies perform worse, supporting signed friction distance margins as an effective mechanism to maintain contact.

topic_matches.title: Omni-IGN: Onboard Image-Goal Navigation for Drones with Omnidirectional Vision
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents Omni-IGN, a fully onboard image-goal navigation system for drones that combines quad-fisheye RGB perception, an attention-based RL policy for continuous control, and a collision-aware safety layer, eliminating the need for dedicated depth sensors. Omni-IGN’s policy adaptively fuses goal-relevant features from multiple omnidirectional views to guide exploration, goal-directed navigation, and obstacle avoidance, and achieves the best performance among continuous-action baselines on Habitat ImageNav benchmarks. In IsaacSim flight tests, integrating learning-based depth estimation with the safety layer improves collision avoidance, and real-world drone experiments demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without fine-tuning or external localization.

topic_matches.title: RAVEN: A Unified Active SLAM System for Rapid Autonomous Visual Exploration with Aerial Robots under Localization Uncertainty
topic_matches.institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces RAVEN, a unified active SLAM framework for quadrotors that jointly plans exploration and loop-closure actions by generating frontier- and loop-closure-based global tour candidates and scoring them with a utility vector that separately quantifies exploration efficiency and localization accuracy, tunable via a prioritization parameter in [0,1]. RAVEN includes a perception-aware navigation planner that produces smooth execution trajectories by minimizing visual state estimation error based on an online Fisher information field capturing real-time visual localization information. Benchmark evaluations show that RAVEN outperforms state-of-the-art active SLAM methods and can realize a spectrum of exploration–localization trade-offs, while fully onboard field experiments with a stereo-inertial quadrotor validate its applicability in challenging environments.

topic_matches.title: VLA-Stem: A Lightweight Safety Mechanism for Vision-Language-Action Models via Reinforcement Learning
topic_matches.institution: Peking University (PKU); University of Macau (UM); University of Science and Technology of China (USTC)
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes VLA-Stem, a lightweight safety mechanism for vision-language-action (VLA) systems that leaves the base VLA policy frozen and instead converts its action chunks into motion references, allowing a learned Stem policy to adjust trajectories and timing at execution while preserving high-level task intent. Conditioned on motion references, robot proprioception, and local obstacle information, the Stem policy is trained via reinforcement learning with teacher–student distillation and curriculum learning to provide trajectory-level guidance that adapts to spatial constraints and dynamic obstacles without degrading base-policy performance in unconstrained settings. Across six constrained simulation scenarios, VLA-Stem attains an average 52.8% collision-free task success rate versus 23.7% for the strongest safety baseline, and real-world experiments similarly show reduced collisions under static and dynamic obstacles while preserving performance in obstacle-free tasks.
